Citycare City of Vaughan/Road patrol plan
Scenario

Road patrol plan built on Ontario's Minimum Maintenance Standards

A class-by-class patrol plan for Vaughan's 1,043 km of municipal roads. Every route can be finished in one sitting, every class is patrolled before its MMS deadline, and the work fits in a fraction of the patrol capacity Vaughan already has.

Prepared by Baseline for Vaughan Public WorksReview meeting, November 5, 2026Depots: 2800 Rutherford Rd; West district 4630 Langstaff Rd in scenario CProposal for review, nothing configured yet

Why we are changing the routes

Ontario Regulation 239/02 sets how often each class of municipal road must be patrolled, and meeting it is what gives Vaughan its statutory defence when a defect leads to a claim. The obligation is per class: Class 3 arterials every 7 days, Class 4 collectors every 14 days, Class 5 local streets every 30 days.

Today's patrol routes in Citycare are large areas that mix every class. A 143 km area takes five to six hours at patrol speed, so it can't be finished in one shift, progress carries over from crew to crew, and busy roads are patrolled no more often than quiet ones.

This plan replaces areas with routes built per road class. Each route starts and ends at 2800 Rutherford Rd, takes three hours or less with travel, covers one class so Citycare repeats it on that class's schedule, and is driven in a set order so the patroller simply follows it to 100%.

What we set out to achieve

Compliance by design

Each class has its own routes and recurrence, so no class can fall behind.

Routes a crew can finish

Three hours or less, so completion is a clear 100% and the next shift starts fresh.

Less capacity than Vaughan has

Patrol takes a few hours of each shift, leaving most of every shift for other work.

Every kilometre counts

Roads driven on the way to a route are recorded as patrolled and taken off other routes.

Driving the road is patrolling

Patrolling a highway "consists of observing the highway, either by driving on or by electronically monitoring the highway" (s. 3(3)). A patroller driving a Citycare route with the app running does exactly that, and every street is time-stamped as it is driven.

What this tells us

Vaughan's classes are sound. Where they differ from the table they are almost always stricter: about 530 km, including 327 km of Class 5 streets that would be Class 6 on traffic alone.

Only 8.4 km are less strict than the table (2.2 km of Class 4 computing as Class 3, 6.2 km of Class 5 computing as Class 4). We kept Vaughan's classes everywhere and flag these for review.

Many traffic counts date from the 1980s to 2000s. New counts could move roads in either direction.

The engineering behind the routes

Patrol routing is a well-studied operations research problem, close to plow and salt routing. These are the steps we ran on Vaughan's network.

Two ways to organize a shift

Same rules, same depot, same three-hour limit. The only difference is where the patroller takes lunch.

Scenario A: two separate loops

Each route is a loop from the office and back. One loop before lunch at the office, one after.

Scenario B: one loop split at lunch

Each shift is one loop cut at a lunch stop: AM from the office to the lunch stop, PM from the lunch stop back. One return trip saved per shift.

Scenario C: scenario B with Vaughan's first feedback

Same lunch-split shifts as B, with the two changes Vaughan officials asked for.

Two operating centresEast district patrols start and end at the Joint Operations Centre, 2800 Rutherford Rd. West district patrols start and end at the Woodbridge/West Operating Centre, 4630 Langstaff Rd.
No Highway 407 ETRCity vehicles don't use the 407. Its mainline and all of its ramps (120 road links) are removed from the network the routes can drive on, so no route uses it, including the west Class 4 route that did.
Districts follow Highway 400Every road is routed from its own district's centre, using Vaughan's east/west of Highway 400 field. Roads driven on the way still count as patrolled.
Shorter trips outWest routes no longer start in Concord, so less of each shift is spent driving to the work and back.

What the comparison shows

Scenario B is more efficient, but modestly: about 6% fewer driving hours (36.4 against 38.9 a week) and about 100 km less driving each week, with full coverage in both.

The gain is small because 2800 Rutherford Rd sits near the centre of the city: returning to the office at mid-day costs only 20 to 40 minutes, and B saves one such trip per shift.

Where B gains: a full Class 5 shift patrols 57 to 71 km of new residential streets, against 50 to 60 km for two separate loops in A.

Scenario C, with the West district running from Langstaff Rd and no 407, needs 35.7 driving hours a week, about 2% less than B and 8% less than A, and about 45 km less driving a week than B. Starting west routes in Woodbridge more than makes up for leaving the 407 out.

What stays the same

Both fit in roughly one patroller-shift a day with the existing pickups, under 20% of the patrol capacity described to us.

In B, three loops are too short to split (Class 2, the last Class 3 and the last Class 4, 1.7 to 1.8 h each). They pair up as a morning loop and an afternoon loop in one shift.

In A, 29 of 31 routes stay on one side of Highway 400. In C every route stays in its own district by design.

In C, splitting by district leaves a few part-shifts: one Class 2 loop per district (0.7 and 1.1 h), and a 45-minute Class 5 loop in the East district once every 28 days.

Why one route on some shifts and two on others

Each route comes due on its own schedule, every 3, 6, 13 or 28 days after it was last done. A shift only gets the routes that are due that day, so some shifts carry one route and others two. No shift ever gets more than two route legs, about 6 hours of driving in 8.

The road patrol plan pays for Category A in about two months

Vaughan runs six patrollers a day, two per shift, three shifts, every day of the year. Today each spends about two-thirds of the shift patrolling. With class-based routes in Citycare, the same MMS coverage takes about one hour per patroller per shift.

Five-year cumulative value against the Category A contract?

What changes, and why it pays?

Today’s patrol areas mix every road class and take five to six hours each, so every patroller spends most of the shift driving, and busy arterials get no more attention than quiet crescents.

The new plan builds routes per MMS class, each under three hours from 2800 Rutherford Rd, repeated on that class’s legal schedule. Roads driven on the way to a route count as patrolled. The whole city is covered with about 5.2 hours of driving a day, plus route prep.

Same six patrollers, same 24/7 coverage, same MMS deadlines. What changes is how much of each 8-hour shift the patrol itself consumes.

One patroller’s 8-hour shift?

Today: two-thirds of the shift, as described by Vaughan. New routes: route driving plus office prep before each route, spread across the six patroller-shifts of a day.

Patrol hours per year?

Why the drop is larger than half

Going from two-thirds of a shift to one-third would already halve patrol time. The routes do better because the full city needs only about 5.2 hours of driving a day once every route is sized to its class and its MMS frequency. Shared across six patroller-shifts, that is under one hour of driving each, plus prep.

Assumptions

  • Patrollers: 2 per shift (east and west of Hwy 400), 3 shifts a day, 365 days. Today each patrols two-thirds of an 8-hour shift, as described by Vaughan.
  • Labour: $45 an hour, applied to patrol hours only.
  • New routes: 1,897 h of route driving a year from the plan (all classes, travel from 2800 Rutherford Rd included) plus 471 h of office prep before routes, from the December 2026 simulation.
  • Distance: 56,171 km a year from the plan. Today’s distance assumes the same average patrol speed as the new routes, about 29.6 km/h.
  • Fuel: pickup trucks at 17 L/100 km and $1.45 a litre. CO2 at 2.3 kg per litre of gasoline.
  • Investment: the Category A contract, $79,925 excluding HST for year one, carried at full value each year with a 3% CPI increase.
  • Not counted: lower vehicle maintenance and wear, overtime avoided, and inflation in wages or fuel. Each would raise the savings.

Annual sidewalk inspection built on O. Reg. 239/02

Every city sidewalk inspected once a year for trip hazards and encroachments, on foot, in loops one inspector can finish in three hours or less.

Prepared by Baseline for Vaughan Public WorksCovers s. 16.1 and s. 16.2 in one passProposal for review, nothing configured yet

Why sidewalks work differently from roads

Roads are patrolled by class, on cycles from twice a week to once a month. Sidewalks have no classes: every sidewalk must be inspected for trip hazards (s. 16.1) and its adjacent area for encroachments (s. 16.2) once per calendar year, never more than 16 months apart.

A 2 cm step can't be judged from a truck, so the inspection is done on foot (or by bike), with a phone. One walk covers both checks. Two ways of grouping the loops are compared: A by City Block, B by density zones.

Winter sidewalk patrol (s. 16.7) is a separate, much lighter program: a representative set of sidewalks, watched mostly from the road during winter road patrols. It is not part of this plan.

What the plan delivers

Every sidewalk, every year

Each loop repeats every 365 days in Citycare, well inside the 16-month limit.

Loops one person can finish

Park, walk the loop, return to the vehicle: three hours or less, two loops a day.

Hazards become tasks

A step over 2 cm creates a repair task due in 14 days; encroachments go to the right department.

Seasonal staffing

One summer student covers the city between May and August.

The standard for sidewalks

O. Reg. 239/02, sections 16.1 to 16.7. What each section asks for, and how this plan or Citycare handles it.

SectionWhat it requiresHow it's handled
16.1 Surface discontinuityInspect every sidewalk once per calendar year, at most 16 months apart. Treat any step over 2 cm within 14 days of knowing.The annual inspection loops in this plan. A step over 2 cm becomes a Citycare task due in 14 days.
16.2 EncroachmentsInspect the area adjacent to each sidewalk once per calendar year, at most 16 months apart.Same walk, same loops. Encroachments are logged as tasks for by-law or forestry.
16.3, 16.4 SnowAfter snow ends, reduce it to 8 cm or less within 48 hours, with at least 1 m of width.Winter maintenance routes (plow routes in the City's file). Not part of this plan.
16.5, 16.6 IceTreat icy sidewalks within 48 hours of becoming aware.Winter maintenance. Not part of this plan.
16.7 Winter patrolWhen snow over 8 cm or ice is likely, patrol sidewalks the City selects as representative, at intervals it decides. Driving by on the road counts.A separate, lighter program, mostly folded into winter road patrols. To be designed with Vaughan.

No classes, no weekly cycles

Unlike roads, the regulation sets no patrol frequency per sidewalk. That is why the sidewalk plan is one yearly program, and why its scenarios only differ in how loops are grouped.

Data notes

Left out: private sidewalks (11 km) and removed segments (3 km). Crosswalk segments are used only to connect loops. 99% of sidewalks are cast-in-place concrete and 97% are 1.5 m wide.

The file doesn't record which road or which side each sidewalk belongs to. We derived it for this analysis; about 300 km of road has sidewalks on both sides and about 600 km on one side.

Inspection plan and season

How the loops are built, how long the program takes, and how it runs in Citycare.

Every loop, in hours

Season: sidewalk km inspected

Starting Monday, May 3, 2027, weekdays only, two loops per inspector per day.

Two ways to group the loops

MeasureA · by City BlockB · density zonesB against A

What differs

The regulation sets no class or priority for sidewalks: each one needs one inspection a year, in any order. A cuts loops inside Vaughan's 51 City Blocks. B ignores those boundaries and builds the densest loops it can, peeling the city from the outside in, then groups them into 16 sectors of 10 loops (one inspector-week each) and 4 zones of 4 sectors (about a month each).

What it means

B needs about 11 fewer hours and 8 fewer inspector-days a year, with no short or broken loops, and its zones and sectors map directly to week-by-week assignments. The saving is modest because most of the extra walking comes from one-sided sidewalks and dead ends. Drop-off and pick-up, or a bike, would save more.

Staffing options

OptionHours a yearPerson-daysFinished by

Bike or e-scooter assumes about 10 km/h while inspecting; Vaughan should confirm a 2 cm step can be judged reliably at that speed.

In Citycare

  • One sidewalk patrol route per loop, named by City Block, in walking order.
  • A recurring task every 365 days from completion, with the 16-month limit as the hard deadline.
  • A step over 2 cm creates a repair task due in 14 days; encroachments create tasks for by-law or forestry.
  • Completion and findings per loop and per inspector in the reporting portal.

Next steps

  • Confirm the inspection mode (on foot or by bike) and the season window.
  • Check the disconnected pieces and whether walkways and multi-use paths are in scope.
  • Design the winter representative set (s. 16.7) with Vaughan.
  • Load the loops in Citycare and start with a two-week pilot.
